# Education in Poland
Education in Poland begins with compulsory primary school (szkoła podstawowa), typically starting at age six or seven and lasting eight years (grades 1–8). Prior to 2017, the system included six years of primary school followed by a three-year junior high school (gimnazjum), but the 2016 education reform abolished gimnazjum, extending primary education to eight years. Before 2019, gimnazjum covered lower secondary education with a broad curriculum including languages, sciences, history, and civics, concluding with evaluations and examinations in humanities, science, and foreign languages. Upper secondary education follows, featuring general secondary schools (liceum) where students attend for four years and can pass the "Matura" exam for university admission, as well as vocational and technical education offered in technical schools (technikum) lasting five years leading to "Matura," or basic vocational schools providing three-year vocational training with certificates. Special schools exist for handicapped students.
Tertiary education aligns with the Bologna system, usually comprising a three-year bachelor’s degree followed by a two-year master’s degree; longer long-cycle programs exist for fields like medicine. Doctoral studies typically take about three years. Vocational education at the tertiary level is conducted through two-and-a-half-year post-secondary schools. University grading uses a numeric scale from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (excellent), with increments of 0.5; grades are awarded each semester based on exams or continuous assessment.
Foreign language instruction is widespread, with English being the most studied (67.9%), followed by German and French. Reforms have mandated learning two foreign languages in lower secondary school. Historically, Poland boasts one of Europe's oldest universities, the Jagiellonian University founded in 1364, and compulsory education was introduced in 1919. The 1999 and 2017 reforms have adjusted school structure and curricula, affecting subjects like history with changing emphases. Educational policies include addressing violence and ensuring compulsory education until age 18.
